title: cuda-graph-segmentation-idle-gap-inference-run-2024-06
body:
Quick notes from a run focused on an odd pattern: repeated short idle gaps between CUDA-graph captured kernel groups during inference microbatching. Goal: understand if segmentation in our capture strategy + small host-device copies are causing SM idle time and lowering effective occupancy.

Background
- Context: production-like inference harness (decoder-only quantized model, 16k context simulated by concatenating prompts). Seeing occasional 15-40ms tail spikes on per-request latency even when overall throughput looks healthy.
- Hypothesis: our current CUDA Graph capture boundaries (we capture per-request segments: embed->decode-init->decode-step->kv-store) create small gaps where streams synchronize or host code polls, resulting in SM idle and lower warp utilization.

Test harness and config
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100-SXM-80GB (driver 535.xx, CUDA 12)
- Binary: serving-runtime/bench/inference_runner:v2024-06-12
- Model: open-llm-small-decoder / 1.3B (8-bit quantized profile)
- Batch shapes: microbatch sizes = [1,2,4], grouped into in-flight slot = 8
- Seq lengths: 8 prefix + 128 gen (most traces use gen length 64)
- CUDA Graph capture: capture per-request segments (4 segments), captured on stream 3, replay on stream 0
- Prefetch: host->device async copies for small tensors (~1-8KB) before each segment
- NVTX marks: marked per-segment start/end and memcpy start/end for correlation in Nsight

Steps taken
1) Collected Nsight Systems (sampling + API tracing) for a 10k request run with microbatch=2.
2) Collected detailed Nsight Compute for hotspot kernels (sm10/inst_counts, warp_efficiency).
3) Enabled timeline-level logging in the runtime for kernel launch times and graph capture boundaries.
4) Instrumented earliest memcpy to log host-pointer alignment and size.

High-level observations
- Repro: idle gaps visible as repeated 0.4-2.5ms holes between groups of short kernels in the timeline. Holes line up with the end of a CUDA Graph segment and before the next replayed graph chunk.
- GPU occupancy per short kernel is high (70-88%) but the overall effective occupancy across the segment is lower because wall-clock time includes the idle holes.
- Warp efficiency drops from ~92% inside long fused kernels to ~75% in the series of small kernels after capture segmentation.
- Small async copies show frequent host staging (pinned buffer allocation hotspots) and occasional 1-2ms page-lock stalls when buffers are not pre-allocated.
- Many of the tiny kernels are <100us; scheduling those back-to-back across different streams seems to induce scheduling jitter and small context-switch gaps.

Example timeline snippet (approx):
- 0.0ms: cudaGraphInstantiate/replay start (segment A) -> fused attention kernel (1.7ms)
- 1.8ms: segment A end, host-side callback does a tiny memcpy (2.0KB) -> async memcpy reported 0.12ms in nvtx but host stalls measured 0.9ms in runtime trace
- 2.7ms: segment B replay -> 6 tiny kernels (0.05-0.12ms each) spread over 0.8ms with 0.3ms idle gaps
- 3.5ms: segment C replay -> persistent kernel invoked (0.9ms)

Telemetry snippets (representative)
- fused_attention_kernel: avg occupancy 81%, warp_eff 92%, sm_eff 78%
- small_matmul_x: avg occupancy 46%, warp_eff 72%
- prefix_memcpy_async: reported 0.12ms device time, but timeline shows host prefetch stall 0.8-1.2ms in 12% of captures

Root-cause hypotheses (ordered)
1) Capture segmentation creates host-side callbacks / control points between segments. Those callbacks perform small synchronous steps (or call into the runtime scheduler) that can block the host thread responsible for queuing the next graph replay, creating gaps.
2) Tiny host->device copies are not fully pre-allocated or aligned, so in some runs the OS-level page pinning costs show up and block the scheduling thread.
3) Using multiple streams for captures + replays means the driver has to preempt/switch contexts for many tiny kernels; the scheduling jitter becomes visible as small gaps.
4) cudaGraph instantiated fragments may not be optimally coalesced by the driver if the captures include different stream dependencies, defeating the kernel launch aggregation benefit.

Short experiments and results tried so far
- Pre-allocate pinned buffers for all small copies: reduced host-side memcpy stalls from ~12% to ~1% of captures. Tail spikes reduced but not eliminated.
- Merge adjacent small memcpy calls into a single larger staged copy: reduced number of tiny kernels but introduced slightly higher peak memory usage. Observed fewer gaps.
- Switch to single stream replay for all graph segments: decreased idle hole occurrences but increased max latency for some requests due to serialized long kernels. Net: tail improved for microbatch=2 but worse for microbatch=4.
- Re-capture a combined graph (A+B) where possible: eliminated the gap between those two segments; however capture size larger and less flexible for dynamic-length behaviors.

Open questions / unknowns
- Are there internal driver heuristics that fragment captures at replay time for certain kernel shapes? Need to reproduce with a minimal standalone harness and file a driver bug if observed.
- Is persistent kernel approach always preferable for short-kernel dominated sequences? It lowers warp-level efficiency for larger ops in some configs.
- What's the best tradeoff for mixing single-stream replay vs multi-stream for mixed long/short kernel workloads?

Immediate recommendations
- Short term (within 2 sprints):
  - Pre-allocate and recycle all pinned staging buffers used by async small copies. (Config flag: prealloc_staging=true)
  - Add an option to prefer coalesced graph captures (capture-combine-adjacent=true) for stable model shapes.
  - Increase in-flight microbatches by +2 for the 1-2ms gap cases to hide small idle holes behind concurrency.
- Medium term (next quarter):
  - Prototype a combined-capture mode that attempts to fuse segments across the hottest path (attention+kv store+decoder-step) and compare cost/latency tradeoffs.
  - Evaluate a persistent kernel runner for the short-kernel tail and measure overall TFLOPS and warp efficiency impacts on a 1B-10B range.
  - Minimal reproduce harness for driver capture fragmentation: isolated kernels (no host-side runtime), single thread queuer -> escalate to NVIDIA if driver-level fragmentation seen.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Create a minimal harness that captures three small kernels with a 2KB memcpy between them and validate driver replay aggregation (nsight-compute + nsight-sys). (owner: Devin)
- Add tracing: record thread scheduling preemption timestamps on host side (clock_gettime) to confirm queuer stall. (owner: Priya)
- Link results to JIRA-ENG-1876 and attach the Nsight timelines + CSV of occupancy slices.

Conclusion
There are multiple contributing factors, but the most actionable wins were preallocating pinned staging buffers and experimenting with capture coalescing. Next step: minimal repro + driver-level validation. If driver is observed to fragment captures unnecessarily, open an escalation with NVIDIA.

Signed-off-by: Liam (notes, rough)
